quote: und dazu wird wahrscheinlich die folgende Funktion [-....-] $f_0(x) = $ [-....-] [-.... x = \sqrt{2}..-] $\left(x - \sqrt{\frac{x^2+1}{2}}\right)^n$
english: and for this purpose the following function will probably serve: f_0(x) = (x - sqrt((x^2+1)/2))^n, with f_1, f_2, ... obtained by differentiating and multiplying by sqrt(x^2+1), f = f_n.
topic: Hilbert considers best approximation of a continuous function by integral functions of the field (x, sqrt(x^2+1)) of the form G(x)+H(x)sqrt(x^2+1), proposes an analogue of Gauss's orthogonality method with a candidate function built by repeated differentiation, and suggests generalizing to arbitrary algebraic function fields and continued fraction expansions.

triage.modern_statement: Take the real hyperbola y^2 = x^2 + 1, i.e. the field Q(x, √(x^2+1)). Its integral functions are G(x) + H(x)√(x^2+1), where G and H are polynomials. The question is how to find the best L2 (least-squares) approximation of a continuous function by such functions on an interval, in analogy with Gauss/Legendre approximation by orthogonal polynomials. In practice this means building an orthogonal basis for this space ordered by degree. Hilbert guesses a Rodrigues-type formula for that basis: start from (x − √((x^2+1)/2))^n and repeatedly differentiate and multiply by √(x^2+1). He then suggests extending the idea to any algebraic function field and linking it to continued fraction expansions (the Abel–Chebyshev theory of hyperelliptic continued fractions and Pell–Abel equations).
triage.answered_by: The general question has been answered in modern work, but Hilbert's specific formula has not been checked. S. Olver and Y. Xu (IMA J. Numer. Anal. 41(1), 2021; arXiv 2018) built explicit orthogonal polynomial bases on every planar quadratic curve, and the hyperbola is one of those curves. Polynomials in (x, y) restricted to y^2 = x^2+1 are exactly the functions G(x) + H(x)y. Fasondini, Olver and Xu (arXiv 2022, and an earlier paper on cubic curves) extended this to curves y^m = φ(x) with m = 1, 2, which covers the hyperelliptic case. I found no source that tests Hilbert's own candidate (x − √((x^2+1)/2))^n with repeated differentiation, or names it as the orthogonal family.

evidence.claim: Olver and Xu study orthogonal polynomials on quadratic curves in the plane and give an explicit orthogonal basis for any quadratic curve. For n ≥ 1 the space of degree-n orthogonal polynomials has dimension 2, which matches the G + H·y structure.
arXiv preprint of the same paper (Orthogonal structure on a quadratic curve), which handles each standard quadratic curve class, including the hyperbola.
Fasondini, Olver and Xu build bivariate orthogonal polynomials on algebraic curves y^m = φ(x) with m = 1, 2. This is the generalization to hyperelliptic function fields.
Recent work on elliptic orthogonal polynomials pushes orthogonal polynomials further onto elliptic curves, which shows the area is still active.
The link to continued fractions in hyperelliptic fields goes back to Abel (1826) and Chebyshev and is still being studied.

triage.why: The research question here is orthogonal bases for least-squares approximation by G(x) + H(x)√(x^2+1). It has been answered: Olver–Xu cover quadratic curves such as the hyperbola, and Fasondini–Olver–Xu cover y^2 = φ(x) curves. Work on orthogonal polynomials on algebraic and elliptic curves, and on hyperelliptic continued fractions, is still going on. Confidence is low for three reasons. I found no source that cites Hilbert's note. I found none that checks whether his Rodrigues-type construction actually gives orthogonal functions. And the transcription is garbled (struck-out text, 'x = √2'). So 'solved' applies to the general problem, not to Hilbert's particular conjecture.
